{"lesson":{"schemaVersion":1,"title":"Lesson 35: Myths, Retellings, and Film Adaptations: Academic Discussion","lessonType":"academic-discussion","header":{"focusStandards":["SL.6.1","SL.6.2","SL.6.6","RL.6.7","RL.6.9"],"supportingStandards":["SL.6.1.a","SL.6.1.b","SL.6.1.c","SL.6.1.d","SL.6.2","SL.6.6","RL.6.7","RL.6.9"],"eldStandards":["ELD.PI.6.1","ELD.PI.6.7","ELD.PII.6.4"],"mediaLiteracyStandards":[],"objectives":[{"kind":"content","text":"Students will synthesize what they have read in the unit to discuss how *The Lightning Thief* retells and reworks traditional myths for a modern audience, and how the film version changes the novel."},{"kind":"language","text":"Students will use academic discourse markers (Building on..., I would like to add..., In contrast..., A recurring pattern is...) and expanded noun phrases to build on peers' ideas and compare the myths, the novel, and the film using evidence from text and film."},{"kind":"foundational-skills","text":"Students will analyze how academic discourse markers support a sustained discussion, and will adapt their speech to a formal academic discussion."}],"essentialQuestions":["How do retellings change across cultures and generations?"],"connections":{"knowledgeBuilding":"Students draw on the myths from Investigations 1 and 2 and on *The Lightning Thief* to see how a story changes when it is retold by a new author, in a new setting, for a new audience. The film clips add a second kind of retelling: a change in medium.","enduringUnderstanding":"Stories travel across cultures and generations, and each retelling changes details, tone, and messages to reflect the values and interests of the people retelling it.","futureLessons":"This discussion prepares students to finish their conversation in the Language Development Huddle/Catch-Up Day (F3), and gives them evidence and language for the cross-text comparison in the culminating writing.","performanceTask":"In Shared Stories, Shared Lessons, students discuss an essential question using evidence from several texts and compare two interpretations of a story. Today's discussion rehearses both skills."},"vocabulary":[{"word":"retelling","definition":"a new version of an existing story told in the teller's own way","tier":"support"},{"word":"adaptation","definition":"a version of a story changed to fit a new form, such as a novel made into a movie","tier":"support"},{"word":"omit","definition":"to leave out","tier":"support"},{"word":"perspective","definition":"the point of view from which something is seen or told","tier":"support"},{"word":"discourse marker","definition":"a word or phrase that signals how your comment connects to what someone else said (for example, *Building on...* or *In contrast...*)","tier":"support"},{"word":"faithful","definition":"staying close to the original","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"The Lightning Thief","author":"Rick Riordan","pages":"Chapters 1-22 (synthesis across the novel; students use their annotated copies and notes)"},{"title":"Myths from Investigations 1 and 2","author":"Various","pages":"Student notes and annotations"},{"title":"Teacher-chosen clips from the movie version of The Lightning Thief","pages":"2-3 short clips, about 2 minutes each, matching scenes students know from the novel"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Students activate what they know about myths and *The Lightning Thief* by recalling one way the novel updates a myth.","activities":[{"id":"launch-turn-and-talk","title":"What Did Riordan Change?","minutes":5,"standards":["SL.6.1"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Take out your novel, your notes on the myths from Investigations 1 and 2, and your notes from the last lesson. Turn and Talk with a partner about the question you hear."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Think about one myth you read earlier in this unit and one scene from *The Lightning Thief*. What is one thing Riordan kept from the myth, and one thing he changed?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Riordan kept the Greek gods and monsters, like the Minotaur and Medusa. But he changed the setting. The gods live above the Empire State Building, and Medusa runs a garden gnome shop. In the old myths nobody is in New York."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Circulate and listen for students who name both a kept element and a changed element. Invite two pairs to share. Keep this to 5 minutes so the discussion time stays protected."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Today you will hold an academic discussion about our essential question: How do retellings change across cultures and generations? First we will talk about myths and the novel. Then we will compare the novel to the film clips."}]}]},{"kind":"literacy-lab","title":"Literacy Lab","purpose":"Students set discussion norms and learn the discourse markers that will help them build on one another's ideas.","activities":[{"id":"lab-norms","title":"Our Discussion Norms","minutes":4,"standards":["SL.6.1","SL.6.1.b","SL.6.6"],"routine":"Think-Pair-Share","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Think about what makes a discussion strong. Share with a partner, then with the class. Help build the norms for today."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What should we see and hear in a discussion where everyone is learning from each other?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Everyone gets a turn to talk, and we listen without interrupting. We use evidence from the book or the movie. We talk about ideas, not about people. We use school language, not slang."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Let's post four norms: Listen without interrupting. Support ideas with evidence from the text or film. Respond to ideas, not people. Use formal, academic language. Formal English means complete sentences and precise words, like *adaptation* and *perspective*."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Display the norms where students can see them during the whole discussion. Assign roles if useful: a Time Keeper per group and a Question Starter who poses the next prompt."}]},{"id":"lab-discourse-markers","title":"Discourse Markers That Keep Talk Going","minutes":6,"standards":["SL.6.1","SL.6.1.c","SL.6.1.d","SL.6.6"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Read the model conversation the teacher displays. Underline each discourse marker, then decide what job it does: adding on, contrasting, or finding a pattern."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Student A: In the myth, the gods are far away and serious. In the novel, Percy talks to Mr. D and Dionysus is grumpy and funny.
Student B: Building on that, the humor makes the gods feel more like real, flawed people.
Student C: In contrast, the myth uses the gods to teach a lesson about power. I would like to add that the novel seems to teach a lesson about belonging.
Student A: A recurring pattern is that Riordan takes a serious myth and makes it personal for a kid."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"These phrases are discourse markers. They tell your listeners how your idea connects to someone else's. *Building on...* and *I would like to add...* grow an idea. *In contrast...* shows a difference. *A recurring pattern is...* pulls many examples together. Without these markers, a discussion turns into a list of separate opinions."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which marker would you use to disagree politely, and why?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I would use *In contrast...* because it shows a different idea without saying the other person is wrong. I could say, 'In contrast, the film shows Percy as older, and that changes how he acts.'"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Keep these on your desk. You will try to use at least two during today's discussion. Notice how strong speakers also use rich noun phrases, such as 'the dangerous, modern setting' or 'a funny, unreliable god', to make their ideas precise."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help multilingual learners notice and rehearse the discourse markers and expanded noun phrases they will use in discussion.","sayAsk":"Say: Let's practice each marker out loud. Say each one chorally, then complete a frame with a partner. Frames: Building on ___'s idea, ___. / I would like to add that ___. / In contrast, ___. / A recurring pattern is ___. Show how to expand a noun phrase: 'the god' becomes 'the grumpy, funny god in the novel.' Ask: What adjective could make your noun phrase more precise?","watchFor":"If students use markers without a complete idea after them, then prompt: What is your idea after *Building on*? If students use only simple nouns, then ask for one descriptive adjective. Emerging: completes one frame with a partner's help and adds a sensory adjective to a noun. Expanding: uses two markers and adds comparative adjectives (more serious, funnier). Bridging: uses markers naturally and embeds a clause in a noun phrase (the god who rules the underworld)."}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Students prepare, then hold a two-part academic discussion: Part 1 on how *The Lightning Thief* reworks myths, and Part 2 on how the film adapts the novel.","activities":[{"id":"lia-prepare","title":"Part A: Preparing Evidence and Modeling","minutes":6,"standards":["SL.6.1","SL.6.1.a","RL.6.9"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief and myth notes from Investigations 1 and 2","pages":"Students' annotated novel (Chapters 1-22) and myth notes"},{"type":"directions","text":"Review your notes and flag one piece of evidence for each of these: setting, character, humor, and point of view. For each, jot what the myth did and what *The Lightning Thief* does. Write the chapter or myth title so you can point to it in the discussion."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Great discussions begin with preparation. Come ready with evidence you can point to, so you can explain where your idea comes from."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Let me model. How does the novel change the cultural message of a myth? I will use a marker as I speak."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In the myths we read, the gods are powerful and demand respect, and heroes prove themselves to the gods. In the novel, Percy is a twelve-year-old who is accused of stealing the lightning bolt and has to fight to be believed. A recurring pattern is that Riordan shifts the focus from honoring the gods to a kid's search for belonging, so the message feels more modern."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.9"],"stem":"Which choice best describes how *The Lightning Thief* reworks traditional Greek myth for a modern audience?","choices":[{"text":"It retells the myths exactly as the ancient Greeks told them.","correct":false,"rationale":"Riordan keeps gods and monsters but puts them in modern settings, so it is not an exact retelling."},{"text":"It keeps mythic gods and monsters but places them in modern America and tells the story through a young hero with humor.","correct":true,"rationale":"Olympus is above the Empire State Building, monsters appear in places like a gnome shop, and Percy's voice is funny and modern."},{"text":"It replaces the gods with ordinary people and takes out the monsters.","correct":false,"rationale":"The gods and monsters stay. Riordan changes where they are and how they act, not whether they exist."},{"text":"It moves the story back to ancient Greece and keeps the same serious tone as the myths.","correct":false,"rationale":"The setting is present-day America and the tone is often humorous, unlike the serious myths."}]},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Distribute the Accountable Talk stems if students have them. Pulse Check answers: keep the discussion brief and use it to clear up any confusion that the novel is a copy of the myths."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in organizing a claim with evidence from the myths and the novel before speaking.","sayAsk":"Say: Plan one claim, one myth detail, and one novel detail. Frame: My claim is ___. In the myth ___, ___. In the novel (Chapter __), ___. This shows ___. Encourage students to rehearse quietly with a partner, in their home language first if helpful, then in English.","watchFor":"If students have evidence from only one source, then prompt: What does the other source show about the same idea? If students retell plot only, then prompt: What changed, and what does that change tell you? Emerging: one detail from the novel using a frame. Expanding: one myth detail and one novel detail with a connecting word. Bridging: a precise claim with both details and chapter or title named."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: finding evidence for setting, character, humor, and point of view","tryThis":"Provide a four-box organizer with one box for each element. Ask students to fill just two boxes, using a myth and a scene they remember. Offer prompts: Where does this scene happen in the myth? Where in the novel? Who is funny, and who is serious?"},{"situation":"Ready for extension: connecting to contemporary values","tryThis":"Ask students to prepare a short idea for how they would reinterpret one myth to express a value important to people today, such as fairness, family, or standing up for friends, and to name what they would change in setting, character, humor, or point of view."}]}]},{"id":"lia-discussion-part1","title":"Part B: Discussion Part 1, Myths and The Lightning Thief","minutes":11,"standards":["SL.6.1","SL.6.1.a","SL.6.1.b","SL.6.1.c","SL.6.1.d","SL.6.6","RL.6.9"],"routine":"Fishbowl","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Form two circles: an inner circle that discusses and an outer circle that listens and takes notes. Inner circle, discuss the prompts for about 5 minutes. Then switch circles for about 5 more minutes. Use the norms and at least two discourse markers. Cite evidence by naming the myth or chapter."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How has *The Lightning Thief* updated, shifted, or reinterpreted traditional mythic elements for a modern audience? Trace at least one example."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I would like to start with the setting. In the myths the gods live on Mount Olympus in Greece. In the novel, Olympus is above the Empire State Building in New York. That updates the myth because readers today know New York, so the old world feels close to ours."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How do setting, character, humor, or point of view change the cultural message of the myths Riordan references?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The myths are told from outside, and the heroes are usually grown-up and famous. In the novel, Percy tells his own story, and he is a kid with dyslexia and ADHD who feels like he does not fit in. Building on that, his sarcasm and the humor make the message about being different and finding your place, instead of about power and glory."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How do communities adapt myths over time? How might you reinterpret a myth to show a value that matters to you today?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Communities change myths so they still matter to the people hearing them. Long ago myths explained nature and taught respect for the gods. A recurring pattern is that each generation keeps the characters but changes the lesson. I would retell a myth about a hero so that friends work together instead of one person doing everything, because teamwork matters to my generation."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Listen for: (1) specific evidence with a chapter or myth named, (2) discourse markers, (3) students paraphrasing a peer before adding their own idea. If the conversation stalls, ask: What does that change tell us about the culture of the people retelling it? Outer circle students should record one idea they heard and one question or response to share when circles switch."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support multilingual learners in contributing evidence-based turns and paraphrasing peers during the fishbowl.","sayAsk":"Say: When you speak, try this order: marker, claim, evidence. Outer circle, write one idea you heard, then say 'I heard you say ___, and I would like to add ___.' Provide frames: One example from the novel is ___. In the myth, ___. In contrast, ___. A recurring pattern is ___. Ask: What word could you add to make your noun phrase more exact?","watchFor":"If a student agrees without adding, then prompt: What evidence supports that idea? If a student drifts to personal stories, then prompt: Connect back to a moment in the myth or novel. Emerging: one turn with a frame and one named detail. Expanding: builds on a peer using a marker and a reason. Bridging: synthesizes two peers' ideas, cites both sources, and uses expanded noun phrases."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: entering the conversation","tryThis":"Give a prepared 'evidence card' with one claim and one detail written ahead of time. Offer a two-step turn: 1) Say your claim with a marker. 2) Read your evidence and say, 'This shows ___.'"},{"situation":"Ready for extension: comparing cultural messages","tryThis":"Ask: Whose values does the retelling reflect, the original culture's or Riordan's readers'? Students must use *In contrast* with evidence from at least two sources."}]}]},{"id":"lia-discussion-part2","title":"Part C: Discussion Part 2, Novel vs. Film","minutes":13,"standards":["SL.6.1","SL.6.1.a","SL.6.1.c","SL.6.1.d","SL.6.2","SL.6.6","RL.6.7","RL.6.9"],"routine":"Fishbowl","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"Teacher-chosen clips from the movie version of The Lightning Thief and the matching novel scenes","pages":"2-3 clips, about 2 minutes each; matching scenes in students' copies of the novel"},{"type":"directions","text":"Watch each clip. Take notes in two columns: What I saw and heard (actors, camera angles, music, special effects) and What I imagined or read in the novel. After each clip, note anything added, left out, reordered, or moved to a new place."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Choose clips of scenes students know well, such as the Minotaur chase, Medusa, or the Underworld. Preview them. If a clip changes the plot a great deal from the novel (for example, Percy is older in the film, and the quest has different objects and some different characters), point students to that evidence as a strong place for comparison. Show clips with captions on if helpful. Allow 5 minutes for viewing and notes, and 8 minutes for discussion in two quick fishbowl rounds."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What did you see and hear in the film that was different from what you imagined when reading? How did those choices change the scene?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"When I read the Medusa chapter, I imagined her voice as creepy and slow. In the film the music got louder and the camera moved close to the actor's face, so it felt more like a horror movie. The special effects made the danger more visual, but the novel's humor with Percy's thoughts was harder to see."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What changed in the adaptation, such as added or removed dialogue, reordered events, or altered settings, and how does it affect characterization, tone, or theme?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In the film, some dialogue was left out, so we do not hear as much of Percy's sarcastic narration. In contrast, the novel lets us inside his head, so he seems funnier and more unsure of himself. The film makes him look more like an action hero, which changes the theme from being an outsider to being a chosen hero."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How well do the clips honor or change the novel? Use evidence from both the text and the film, and build on a classmate's idea."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Building on what Maria said, the film keeps the main events, like the monster attack, so it honors the plot. But I would like to add that it changes the tone, because the novel is funny and the clip is more serious. I think it is faithful to the action but not to the voice of the book."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Press for specific film evidence ('the camera zooms in,' 'the music gets faster') and specific text evidence (a chapter or a quoted line). Remind students that SL.6.2 is about explaining how the film information contributes to the topic: what does the media show that the text does not, and vice versa?"},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help multilingual learners describe what they see and hear in the film, compare it with the novel, and evaluate the language and media choices.","sayAsk":"Say: Use sense words for the film: loud, dark, close-up, fast. Use frames: In the film, I saw/heard ___. In the novel, ___. In contrast, ___. The film is more/less ___ than the novel because ___. Ask: Which choice, the music, the camera, or the dialogue, changed the scene most, and why? Let students pre-write one sentence about each clip.","watchFor":"If students say only 'the movie was better/worse,' then prompt: What is one specific choice that made you feel that way? If students compare without evidence, then prompt: Point to a line or a moment. Emerging: names one thing they saw or heard and one thing in the novel with a frame. Expanding: compares one change with a reason using *because* or *in contrast*. Bridging: evaluates how well the film honors the novel using precise language and expanded noun phrases (the fast, tense music; a more serious tone)."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: describing film techniques","tryThis":"Give a word bank: close-up, music, special effects, acting, setting. Ask students to pick one and complete: In the clip, the ___ makes the scene feel ___. In the novel, I imagined ___."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: evaluating the adaptation","tryThis":"Ask: If you were the director, what one change would you make so the film better honors the novel's voice? Defend it with evidence from both the text and the clip, using *I would like to add* and *In contrast*."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students reflect on the discussion and write one insight about how retellings change.","activities":[{"id":"lookback-quick-write","title":"Quick Write: How Retellings Change","minutes":5,"standards":["SL.6.1.d","RL.6.9"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Write two or three sentences in response to the prompt. Use at least one discourse marker and name the text or film you are referring to."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What is one idea from today's discussion that helps answer the question: How do retellings change across cultures and generations?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Building on today's discussion, I learned that retellings change the setting, the humor, and the point of view to fit the people hearing them. Riordan moved the Greek gods to New York, and the film changed the tone with music and camera angles. A recurring pattern is that each retelling keeps the main characters but changes the message."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Collect the Quick Writes to see who can name both a change and its effect. Use them to decide who to pull into small groups during the next Flex Day, when students finish their Academic Discussion."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework (Optional)","purpose":"Students rehearse for the continued discussion.","activities":[{"id":"homework-prepare","title":"Prepare Evidence for Continued Discussion","minutes":0,"standards":["SL.6.1.a"],"routine":"Journal","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"In your journal, write one question you still have about how the film or novel changes a myth. Then write two pieces of evidence, one from the novel or a myth and one from the film clips, that you could use to answer it. Practice saying your idea aloud using one discourse marker."}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"Students held a two-part academic discussion on the essential question 'How do retellings change across cultures and generations?' Part 1 compared *The Lightning Thief* with myths from Investigations 1 and 2, and Part 2 compared the novel with teacher-chosen film clips, using discourse markers and evidence from text and film.","keyActivities":["Turn and Talk: what Riordan kept and changed from myths","Co-constructing discussion norms and learning discourse markers (Building on, I would like to add, In contrast, A recurring pattern is)","Part A: preparing evidence and a teacher model with a Pulse Check on how the novel reworks myth","Part B: Fishbowl discussion on how setting, character, humor, and point of view change the myths' messages","Part C: Fishbowl discussion comparing film clips with the novel (what students saw and heard versus what they imagined)","Quick Write on how retellings change"],"vocabularyTaught":["retelling","adaptation","omit","perspective","discourse marker","faithful"],"standardsCovered":["SL.6.1","SL.6.2","SL.6.6","RL.6.7","RL.6.9","SL.6.1.a","SL.6.1.b","SL.6.1.c","SL.6.1.d","ELD.PI.6.1","ELD.PI.6.7","ELD.PII.6.4"]}}
